t: Section 102(c)(1) of the Renegotiation Act of 1951 (50 U.S.C. App., sec. 1212(c)(1)) is amended by striking out “June 30, 1971” and inserting in lieu thereof “June 30, 1973”.

fable.w: This section only extends a termination date in the Renegotiation Act of 1951 by replacing one date with another. One might be tempted to read participation into it because the Renegotiation Act involves contractors dealing with a federal board, but this text itself creates no consultation, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue involving any party outside the federal government.
fable.s: is amended by striking out “June 30, 1971” and inserting in lieu thereof “June 30, 1973”

qwen_block.w: This section is a simple technical amendment that updates a date in an existing statute. It does not establish any process for consultation, public comment, advisory boards, or coordination with outside parties. It merely changes a deadline or effective date within the federal government's own regulatory framework.
qwen_block.s: Section 102(c)(1) of the Renegotiation Act of 1951 (50 U.S.C. App., sec. 1212(c)(1)) is amended by striking out “June 30, 1971” and inserting in lieu thereof “June 30, 1973”.

opus.w: The section only replaces one date with another in the Renegotiation Act of 1951. It sets up no way for anyone outside the federal government to take part in a federal decision: no comment period, hearing, rulemaking authority, advisory body, consultation or right to sue. The Act's general link to renegotiating contracts does not change that, because this section creates no process at all.
opus.s: is amended by striking out “June 30, 1971” and inserting in lieu thereof “June 30, 1973”.
opus.b:
This section only changes a date: it pushes the deadline in Section 102(c)(1) of the Renegotiation Act of 1951 from June 30, 1971 to June 30, 1973.

The tempting wrong reading is that the Renegotiation Act involves contractors negotiating with the government, so outsiders might seem to take part. But this section creates no comment period, hearing, rulemaking authority, advisory body, consultation or right to sue. The answer is therefore "No."

qwen_chat.w: This section is a simple amendment that changes a specific date in an existing statute. It does not establish any advisory committees, public comment periods, consultations with states or tribes, or any other mechanism for outside parties to participate in federal decision-making. It is purely an administrative update to a deadline.
qwen_chat.s: Section 102(c)(1) of the Renegotiation Act of 1951 (50 U.S.C. App., sec. 1212(c)(1)) is amended by striking out “June 30, 1971” and inserting in lieu thereof “June 30, 1973”.

It does not create any new process for consulting with outside parties, nor does it involve any interaction with non-federal entities. The text is purely a date substitution.
